bearings.paper_claim: Platform text for 5,228 of 6,016 (86.9%) major-party ballot-eligible House primary candidates 2018-2022, with 43,465 hand-topic-coded platform points. Identifiers are FECCandID (not universal) and BioGuideID (incumbents only).
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.1; Methods p.4; Data Records p.5; Usage Notes p.9-10 (ID caveats)
bearings.system_side: build_electoral_plays.py: the contest route primary term takes, per category, the Opponent's shortfall against the same-party average avgP, keeps only the negative parts, and divides the sum by the number of categories. So it is a mean-style proxy, not a plain sum. No challenger data enters.
bearings.transfer_conditions: House only, 2018-2022 cycles; the 14 topic codes are not CU categories. BioGuideID is incumbent-only and the paper advises against aggregating by either ID. Challenger coverage gaps (low fundraising, uncompetitive races) are where the proxy matters most. New analysis stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Count and coverage figures reproduce exactly. The keying claim is overstated: the paper says BioGuideID exists only for incumbents and FECCandID is missing for some. The contest route uses a mean-style shortfall over categories, not a plain sum. The substance (same-party average proxy, no real challenger data) holds.

bearings.paper_claim: Each platform point is hand-coded by trained annotators to one of 14 Major Policy Topic codes using a codebook. A 20% relabel (8,584 points, by 2022 coders) gave 80% agreement, Cohen kappa 0.84 and weighted kappa 0.74, with most disagreement on Unknown/Other.
bearings.system_side: cu_press_release_scraper.R defines 19 Layer-2 categories by regex term lists plus bill-based tags. detect_categories tags a release with EVERY category it touches, so the tagger is multi-label, not single-topic. A human-label kappa exists for stance (run_stage5.R line 133: regex 0.17, DEBATE 0.34). No topic-level reliability benchmark was found.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Transfers as a validation design (double-code a random sample, report kappa), not as labels: genre and topic scheme differ from CU categories. The paper's single-topic rule under-codes multi-topic text, but the regex tagger does not share that rule.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper figures reproduce. The claim that the regex tagger shares the single-topic-per-item rule is refuted by detect_categories, which is multi-label. The claim that no human benchmark exists is too strong: a stance kappa exists in run_stage5.R. Only the topic-level absence is supported, and only by a keyword search.

bearings.paper_claim: Cross-cycle candidate names linked by probabilistic record linkage on pretrained embeddings, blocked on party and state. Estimated matches under 50% were hand-checked: 15 wrong for 2018-2020, 1 for 2020-2022, none for 2018-2022.
bearings.system_side: member_identity.py Resolver (about lines 118-135) maps a bioguide ID to a roster name and returns None as a refusal rather than guessing. The cited lines contain no contributor rule ladder (name parts, zip, city, occupation, employer) and no name-frequency logic, and a keyword search of member_identity.py found no occupation or employer rules.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper links candidates (a small, ID-rich population), not donors; its error counts do not speak to donor-level false-match rates. Member bioguide lookup is a different problem from cross-cycle name linkage.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper figures reproduce exactly. The contributor-ladder and no-name-frequency-weighting claims are unsupported at the cited lines and were not found in member_identity.py. Only the Resolver bioguide and refusal behavior stands.

related.why: Vault summary confirms Bonica's CFscores are donor-based candidate ideal points. The pairing with CampaignView platform text is the analyst's suggestion; the paper does not cite Bonica.
Vault title and summary confirm a study of when moving to the middle wins votes. CampaignView is a candidate-level source of primary positions, as the analyst says; the paper does not cite Broockman.

Vault file confirms it is about LLMs for political texts (Political Science Research and Methods, 2025). The analyst's use as a scalable check on CampaignView's hand codes is a suggestion, not a claim in either paper.

summary_issues: Coverage: all 3 bearings and all 3 related links were checked against the paper text and code. Paper figures in the summary (5,228/6,016, 86.9%, 43,465, 8,584, 80%, kappa 0.84, 0.74, 15/1/0 wrong matches, 11.9%, 25.1%, one-week scrape, 7.8% Wayback) reproduce.

Keying: the summary says platform text is keyed by FEC ID and BioGuideID. The paper says BioGuideID exists only for incumbents, FECCandID is missing for some, and aggregation by either is not recommended.
Relabel scope: the summary omits that the 20% relabel was done only on 2022 primary text by coders from that cycle. The reliability statistics therefore cover one cycle only.

Missingness direction: the summary's claim that unopposed and better-funded candidates are less likely to be missing matches Table 5 signs. But the paper's prose says contested-primary candidates are less likely to be missing, which contradicts its own table. The summary should flag this internal inconsistency.
Missingness pooling: Table 5 coefficients are pooled across parties and cycles. The summary should quote them as UNSTRATIFIED associations.

Contest route: the summary says the proxy is a sum of negative gaps against the same-party average. The code divides by the number of categories, so it is a mean-style shortfall. The summary also omits the general (cross-party) route, which takes the max of the two.

Tagger: the summary says the single-topic-per-item caveat also applies to the regex press-release tagger, and that no human benchmark exists. Both are refuted or overstated by the Draft Systems code (multi-label tagging; stance kappa in run_stage5.R line 133).
Scrape timing: the summary says text was scraped about one week before each primary. The paper also runs searches one month before and after the season, so the window is wider than one week.
